candidates.title: Folio: Recoverable Multi-Resolution Context Folding for Long-Horizon Language Agents
candidates.author: Yubo Ruan et al.
candidates.organization: Baidu, Inc.; Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
candidates.what_changed: A context manager that replaces model-written compaction/summarization with programmatic folding over pre-recorded multi-resolution history, plus handle-based recovery tools.
candidates.mechanism: While the agent runs it records three linked levels: L1 short turn notes the model writes inside its normal reply, L2 a runtime-written event manifest of every call, L3 the captured source records. Folding selects coarser views for older turns (no model call), printing handles into L2/L3; recovery tools 'scan' (bounded page reads) and 'ctx' (run shell/Python over full text in files) plus a persistent dossier reach folded evidence. A 'landing-priced' fold trigger (rent-or-buy view of prompt-cache cost) decides when to fold and includes a retained budget L. Demotion is monotone so the folded prefix stays cache-friendly.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium. 75 LOCA-bench tasks (15 environments x 5 seeds) run as five 15-task chained sessions; each system runs each chain once; one model (DeepSeek-V4-Pro) behind every system; paired exact McNemar tests. Significant vs same runtime with model compaction (p=0.004) and vs SoL-Pi (p<0.001); NOT significant vs Claude Code (p=0.19) or Codex (p=0.06). Chain-to-chain variance is 3-4 of 15 tasks. Benchmark contamination scan flagged runs for all systems (Folio 8, Claude Code 9, Codex 27, SoL-Pi 24, Piki-Classic 11) and flagged runs were kept.
candidates.independent_confirmation: None; authors' own runtime (Piki) and evaluation.
candidates.relevance: high - direct context-engineering result with cost accounting under prompt caching; challenges summarize-to-compact as default in agent harnesses.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: None direct. Adjacent to prior agent memory provenance piece (recoverable records/handles) but distinct topic (context compaction).
candidates.summary: Setup: LOCA-bench, an open benchmark of tool-using tasks whose context grows with the environment (course scheduling from Canvas/email, WooCommerce inventory/sales, invoice checking, A/B-test analysis, etc.), 15 environments x 5 seeds = 75 tasks with deterministic graders. Five chains: chain k takes seed k of every environment and runs its 15 tasks sequentially in one session so later tasks inherit earlier history. 60 of 75 tasks triggered at least one fold; median context at fold 242K tokens. Systems, all on DeepSeek-V4-Pro with 1M windows: Folio in the Piki runtime (L=50K landing budget), Folio with 128K window, Piki-Classic (same runtime, model-written summary at 90% of window), Claude Code, Codex, SoL-Pi. Results: Folio (1M) solved 66/75 (13.2 +/- 1.5 per chain) vs Claude Code 59, Codex 57, Piki-Classic 54, SoL-Pi 49; Folio-128K solved 60. Paired vs Piki-Classic: 14 tasks only Folio solved vs 2 only Piki-Classic solved (p=0.004). Vs Claude Code 14 vs 7 (p=0.19, not significant); vs Codex 14 vs 5 (p=0.06); vs SoL-Pi 20 vs 3 (p<0.001). Gap concentrated in two environments (NHL B2B analysis: Folio 4/5, all others 0/5; A/B test 4/5 vs at most 2/5). Mean working time 10.2 min/task vs 16.3 (Piki-Classic), 18.5 (Claude Code), 20.2 (Codex), 21.0 (SoL-Pi). Normalized cost (cached-read equivalents h+30u+90o using DeepSeek price ratios) 1,481M vs 3,525M tokens over 75 tasks for Piki-Classic, i.e. 2.38x cheaper; cheaper on 68/75 tasks. Closed agents expose no usage so their cost is not compared. Fold median 0.6 s; across 809 folds none issued a model request and a re-render consistency check found one mismatch (in a discarded run). Agent made 315 ctx calls, 55 scan calls and 86 handle expansions in main runs; 6.7% of ctx calls exited nonzero. Ablations: removing dossier changed one success, removing L1 notes three; removing scan/ctx on one chain dropped 13 to 8 successes (confounded by timeouts/retries). Limitations (authors): one benchmark, one model, one price structure, single run per chain; ablations on one chain; L1 notes and dossier are model-written and can be wrong; ctx executes model-written commands and its isolation is not evaluated; recoverability does not imply the agent uses the right evidence.

candidates.title: Cleaning an Agent's History Hurts When the World Still Holds the Error
candidates.author: Egor Pakhomov et al.
candidates.what_changed: Controlled evidence that history edits used by compaction/repair/handoff can hurt agents when the edited record disagrees with persistent world state.
candidates.mechanism: Freeze an agent mid-task with exact restorable world state, edit either the history (record) or the world, and let a receiver model continue. Contrast a truthful note beside a preserved error vs rewriting the history to show the agent's own completed correct action; on AppWorld, cross success/failure receipt with whether the DB write's effect is present.
candidates.evidence_quality: High for a controlled study: pre-written estimands, restoration certified (AgentCE-Bench 200/200 identical replays), task-cluster bootstrap (10,000 draws); 319 frozen states, 2,552 continuations on AgentCE-Bench; 1,040 continuations in 260 four-cell blocks on AppWorld over 65 task families. Caveats: authors choose states and edits; only two receivers carry the primary result; 24-step budget binds unevenly (71.4% of continuations use all steps); two preregistered analyses had to be reimplemented; targeted control incomplete (provider refused 45 units).
candidates.independent_confirmation: None; cites related work (Lin et al. 2026 diagnostic annotations) with consistent direction.
candidates.relevance: high - directly actionable for context compaction, self-repair and multi-agent handoff design: judge history-management policies against world state, not transcript tidiness.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Touches themes of agent memory provenance and multi-agent handoffs but is a distinct, new experimental result.
candidates.summary: Receivers: gpt-5.5 and claude-sonnet-5 on both designs; AppWorld adds gpt-5, gpt-5-mini, gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini, gemini-3.1-pro-preview, grok-4.6 (eight receivers, four providers). Difficulty calibrated per receiver to a 25-75% success band (claude-sonnet-5 sat below band on AppWorld and was kept as a named below-band receiver). Design 1, AgentCE-Bench (grid-filling tool environments): 319 states frozen two-thirds through a task after a wrong value was committed to persistent state. Arms add the same verified-correct value two ways. Truthful note beside the preserved error raised recovery (share of remaining look-ahead targets correct) from 51% (matched neutral note) to 66%. Rewriting history to show the agent's own completed correct action lowered recovery below the unedited history, 50% to 44% - so presence of the correct value does not predict the effect. Design 2, AppWorld: freeze after a database write; keep the original success receipt or swap in a failure receipt, and independently set the DB to pre- or post-write state. A success receipt lowered whole-task success from 45% to 28% when the effect was absent and raised it from 38% to 49% when present; interaction differs by 27 points pooled over two receivers, positive in six of eight receivers at 97.5% and seven at 95%. Diagnostic: under a success receipt, re-issue rate of the focal request fell from 52.69% to 10.38% once effect was present. Natural occurrence: of 1,350 AgentCE-Bench source episodes, 1,074 called done and in 393 of those the world held a wrong value the agent's own receipt had confirmed. Practical claim: a record made to look clean while the world holds the error left agents worse off than no edit; a success receipt over an absent effect cost 17 points vs a failure receipt. Limitations (authors list eight): truth and channel not crossed; AppWorld receipts differ in content as well as truth; uneven step budget; few receivers; one note wording/one receipt string; states are the authors' selection; no actual compaction or handoff policy tested; nothing bounds an adversary; all receivers are closed API models whose versions can change.

candidates.title: When Evaluators of AI Agents Disagree: An Empirical Study of Native Scoring, LLM Judges, and Commit-Boundary Checks on tau2-bench
candidates.author: Sungbin Im
candidates.organization: Seoul School of Integrated Sciences and Technologies (aSSIST); present address AIM Intelligence
candidates.what_changed: Measures that LLM-as-judge and benchmark native scoring are not interchangeable for tool-using agents, and that LLM judges pass nearly all forbidden database writes that a no-model rule check catches.
candidates.mechanism: Records every WRITE tool call in tau2-bench airline/retail. Four evaluators: native gold-state scoring; LLM judge on transcript; judge given policy doc (judge-P); a 'boundary evaluator' that compares whether the gold task expected a write with whether a non-error write occurred. Also tests three pre-write gates (verification, correction, safe termination) via a wrapper around the unmodified benchmark.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium. 2,160 episodes (90 tasks x 2 models x 4 gate conditions x 3 reps), task-cluster bootstrap, Holm-corrected permutation tests; human reference of 120 stratified episodes by two annotators. Weaknesses: single author; second annotator from same organization; only 11 confirmed premature commitments; agents and judges all OpenAI gpt-4.1 family (one top-tier gpt-5.6 Sol judge on labeled subset); judge input truncated (re-run untruncated did not change result); A2 agreement only 0.650 raw in round 1. Total API cost ~USD 93; traces/code/labels released.
candidates.independent_confirmation: Partially consistent with prior work cited: Rabinovich et al. 2026 (8-17% latent policy violations in tau2 airline) and Advani 2026 (judge AUROC <=0.65 on 9,876 tau2 trajectories).
candidates.relevance: high - evaluation practice for deployed agents; cheap deterministic commit-boundary checks vs LLM judges.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Related to agent observability (traces) and Anthropic safety-evaluations piece, but distinct empirical result on judge validity.
candidates.summary: Benchmark: sierra-research/tau2-bench at commit 363133a; airline 50 tasks, retail 40 test-split tasks. Agent models gpt-4.1-mini and gpt-4.1; simulated customer and gate verifier gpt-4.1-mini; judge gpt-4.1-mini at temp 0.4 with 2 calls/episode. Results: judge self-agreement 98.2% but agreement with native scoring only 56.2%. Eleven human-confirmed premature commitments (forbidden writes, e.g. cancelling a reservation policy forbids): the judge passed 10-11 of 11 with or without policy doc or untruncated transcript; strongest judge still passed 6; the boundary evaluator (no model call) caught all 11; no judge significantly exceeded it on human labels. With the policy document the top-tier judge caught all 11 but failed most actually-correct episodes. Premature commitments occurred in 11.1% of ungated episodes (airline 19.3%, retail 0.8%). Gates gave no significant reduction after multiple-comparison correction; traced cause: the gates' evidence digest dropped order status and customer authentication, so valid requests were rejected. Wrapper sanity check: mean native reward 0.36 with and without wrapper (C0), 7 vs 7 discordant episodes. Human labels: round-1 A1 raw agreement 0.842 (kappa 0.686), A2 0.650; 62 episodes adjudicated. Limitations: two customer-service domains, one repo commit, two models of one family; boundary evaluator only checks that a write occurred, not its content, and depends on gold annotation of whether a write is expected - so it needs gold info that deployments also lack, which the author acknowledges limits it to the logic structure rather than numbers transferring.

candidates.title: OverServe: Resource Amplification Attacks on SaaS Agents via Tool--Prompt Co-Design
candidates.author: Ruiheng Yu et al.
candidates.organization: Florida State University; Johns Hopkins University
candidates.what_changed: A denial-of-wallet style attack where a malicious tenant pairs an innocuous-looking MCP status tool with a completion-confirmation prompt so the agent keeps polling after the business task is done.
candidates.mechanism: Each tool call returns accurate status and terminates normally, but the prompt makes completion conditional on a status that stays 'pending' ('churn'), so the agent repeatedly checks. Because the malicious intent is split across tool and prompt, each passes separate screening. A multi-agent framework writes service-specific tool-prompt pairs, runs static/prompt review, and selects candidates.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium-low for generality: selected tasks from nine benchmarks plus Terminal-Bench, controlled backend simulations of incomplete synchronization; aggregation mixes updated selected cases with earlier condition medians; reported maxima are under benchmark-specific caps. Strong on stealth claim: 5 industrial MCP scanners flagged 0 of 22 crafted tools; research detectors DCI and Connor flagged 3 and 1.
candidates.relevance: high - AI operations/security for multi-tenant agent SaaS; cost-exhaustion threat that passes task checks and MCP scanners.
candidates.summary: Victims: Qwen3.8-27B, Nemotron-3-Super, local DeepSeek-v4-Flash, Sonnet-5 on Bedrock (plus Gemini-3.8-Flash and hosted DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash in appendix). Writers/reviewers: gpt-5.6-sol or glm-5.3-flash. Benchmarks: MCPMark, BrowseComp-Plus, STATE-Bench, EnterpriseOps-Gym (EOG), Enterprise-Worlds, WorkBench, Toolathlon-GYM, AppWorld, TheAgentCompany, Terminal-Bench. Results: across five enterprise workflow benchmarks, 20 victim-benchmark entries give geometric mean amplification 10.30x (Qwen 19.30x, Nemotron 8.07x, local DeepSeek 17.75x, Sonnet 4.07x). At the 200-iteration cap Qwen raised EOG calls from 5 to 200 (40x); local DeepSeek 33.5x. Max: Sonnet on AppWorld 93.88x API-request amplification. Terminal-Bench elapsed-time amplification 12.12x-53.48x. WorkBench with Nemotron: 2 to 16 calls (8x), all nine attacked runs pass native checks. Versus prior attacks (A2M, LoopTrap, Sponge Tool Attack) on MCPMark/EOG with 40-turn budget: OverServe 1.25-1.50x in quiet runs, 7-10x under churn, all 24 runs pass task checks; LoopTrap also reaches 10x but with 2-10x quiet overhead and is detected by source review/Connor; A2M 1.17-1.50x; STA <2x. Median token increase 8.70x vs matched clean runs. Scanners evaluated include Cisco AI Defense MCP Scanner (v4.8.4, YARA analyzer) and MCP-Shield among five industrial scanners. Limitations: selected tasks only, simulated backends, original task checks do not check the added synchronization requirement; review inputs and baseline adaptations vary across experiments. Mitigation implication: per-tenant budgets/loop caps and completion criteria not controllable by tenant prompts.

candidates.title: Termination Lag: Coding Agents Solve Early but Stop Late
candidates.author: Musa Cim et al.
candidates.what_changed: Quantifies how many steps coding agents spend after their first correct patch, by snapshotting and testing the repo patch after every step.
candidates.mechanism: Record repository patch after each agent step, evaluate every distinct patch offline against benchmark tests; define time-to-first-correct-patch (TTFCP) and termination lag (steps after it); classify post-solution steps (verification, exploration, editing, wrap-up).
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium. Five models, two frameworks (OpenHands primary, mini-SWE-agent), SWE-bench Verified (500), Multilingual (300), Pro; each task run once; steps used as cost proxy, not tokens/compute; oracle stopping uses hidden tests agents can't see, so savings are an upper bound.
candidates.relevance: medium-high - agent cost/latency and stopping-rule design; also an eval point (final-patch score hides when it was solved).
candidates.summary: Models: Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B and Laguna-XS.2 (core; Verified and Multilingual, 100/250 step budgets, 131K/256K context), Seed-OSS-36B on SWE-bench Pro (150 steps), Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna on Verified (100 steps); open models served with vLLM on Argonne's Aurora. Findings: 38-82% of successful runs had a correct solution on their initial source-code edit (82% for Qwen3-Coder on Verified). In successful runs a median 35-37% (Qwen3-Coder) and 54-60% (Laguna-XS.2) of steps come after the first correct patch on Verified and Multilingual. Oracle stopping at first correct patch would remove a median 35%/37% of steps (Qwen3-Coder Verified/Multilingual), 60%/54% (Laguna-XS.2), 54% (Haiku on Verified) while preserving every solved task. Mini-SWE-agent: median lag 12 steps, normalized 37%. Post-solution steps are mostly verification and repository exploration; in 1-8% of cases continued activity undoes the correct patch, leaving the final answer wrong. Limitations: one run per task; 1-4% of solved runs hit step/context limit; rule-based step categories; Seed-OSS on Pro solves few tasks. Authors frame termination lag as an upper bound on savings for any practical stopping rule.

candidates.title: Read Once, Answer Many: Parallel Prompting for Shared-Context LLM Inference
candidates.author: Zekun Zhao, Jeffrey Flanigan
candidates.what_changed: Open-source SGLang modification that decodes many independent questions over one shared long document as parallel streams of a single request, reading the document KV once per decode step.
candidates.mechanism: Prefix caching removes redundant prefill but each decode step still reads the shared KV once per question. Parallel Prompting packs P question streams into one request; an in-kernel stream-id attention mask keeps each answer conditioned only on document + its own question; positions start right after the document so RoPE matches single-question requests; fixed decode shapes keep CUDA-graph capture. ~80 lines across three SGLang files plus a small engine package.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium-high for the targeted workload: 144/144 paired runs faster (2 GPUs x 2 SGLang releases x 6 workloads x 6 input sets); accuracy parity checked on QuALITY, LooGLE, SQuAD. Narrow scope: offline/batch only, single GPU, Triton backend only, greedy decoding.
candidates.relevance: medium-high - inference/serving technique for document QA, labeling, and LLM-as-judge batch evaluation workloads.
candidates.summary: Implemented on SGLang v0.5.22 and v0.4.2.post3; A100-SXM4-80GB and RTX A6000. Synthetic grid: CodeLlama-7B-Instruct, 8k-16k-token documents, 64-256 questions/document, 128 output tokens: 3.7x faster than stock SGLang+FlashInfer on A100 and 5.9-6.0x on A6000; 256 questions on 16k doc: 5.0x (A100) and 7.4-8.5x (A6000). Speedup falls with longer outputs: 3.6x to 1.9x on A100 going 128 to 1024 output tokens. GQA models (Qwen2.5 7B-32B): 1.3-1.9x. Real benchmarks with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on v0.5.22: QuALITY (2,086 questions, 115 articles, ~5.7k tokens) answered in 73.6 s, 1.81x faster than stock FlashInfer, 2.12x vs Triton; LooGLE (20k-token docs, long 234-token answers): 1.12x faster than Triton but 1.26x SLOWER than stock FlashInfer. Accuracy/recall within 0.33 points (QuALITY) and 0.36 (LooGLE); SQuAD v1.1 EM/F1 CIs include zero. Continuous-batching variant: 1.22x faster with 32% fewer decode steps on mixed-length answers. Limitations: batch/offline only (needs online scheduler integration), one attention backend, single GPU, greedy decoding; benefit shrinks with long/variable answers, small KV-per-token models, or faster baseline kernels; outputs not bitwise identical.

candidates.title: Cited but Unused: Parametric Provenance in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.author: Tanzeel Abbas et al.
candidates.organization: COMSATS University Islamabad; Middlesex University London
candidates.what_changed: Shows RAG citations often attach to claims the model answered from parametric memory, and that NLI-based citation verification cannot detect it (chance-level AUROC).
candidates.mechanism: Counterfactual value substitution: replace a value appearing in both answer and retrieved passages with a false variant throughout passages and regenerate; if the model still reports the original value, the claim is parametric. Compares ten attribution methods; best signal is contrast between model distribution with vs without context.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium. ASQA with GTR top-5 retrieval, 800 questions per condition, greedy decoding, single seed; claim-level bootstrap. Only open models 0.5B-14B; 19-24% of records undetermined and discarded; protocol covers only claims with a shared numeric value (~70% of ASQA answers, 16.5%/21.8% of ELI5/QAMPARI); ELI5/QAMPARI yield 4 and 3 parametric cases.
candidates.relevance: high - RAG evaluation: citation-support checks used in production can certify post-rationalised citations.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Partial thematic overlap with prior 'agent memory provenance' coverage (provenance), but this is RAG citation faithfulness, not agent memory.
candidates.summary: Models: Qwen2.5-Instruct 0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B/14B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (bf16). Parametric share of citable claims on ASQA rises within Qwen from 1.2% (0.5B) to 13.3% (14B) (Kendall tau 0.80, driven by endpoints); Llama-3.1-8B 15.7% vs Qwen2.5-7B 8.2%. At the most conservative substitution distance: 4.6% and 8.5% on the two models tested. ELI5 4.5% (4 of 89 decided), QAMPARI 2.4% (3 of 124) on Qwen2.5-7B. Among models above 1.5B, 89-100% of parametric claims still carry a citation, within a few points of contextual claims. DeBERTa NLI verifier (max entailment over passages): every bootstrap interval contains 0.5; cited-passage-only check on Qwen2.5-7B AUROC 0.532 [0.415, 0.646] over 408 cited claims; mean entailment actually higher for parametric claims (0.329 vs 0.214) even though the cited passage contains the asserted value in 0 of 35 parametric cases. Best detector (with/without-context distribution contrast) separates provenance but acting on it does not improve 'provenance honesty' at these base rates; authors say it measures what the model knew, not what it used. Requires token logprobs, so not applicable to closed frontier APIs as-is. Extrapolation to larger models untested.

candidates.title: PolicySniff: Inferring Agent Policy States through Shared-GPU Execution
candidates.author: Weimin Fu et al.
candidates.organization: Lehigh University; New York University; NYU Abu Dhabi
candidates.what_changed: A co-resident GPU timing side channel that infers which confidential approval policy (ask-before-execute vs execute) an MoE-served agent is running, even when outputs are identical.
candidates.mechanism: Policy text in the cached prefix changes MoE expert routing for the subsequent task suffix; on an eager MoE runtime dispatching each expert separately, this changes GPU time-slice occupancy that an attacker process measures by timing its own busy-loop kernel with CUDA events (no profiler/NVML). Attacker profiles both candidate settings per known task first.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium. Frozen, hash-committed, blinded coverage study on one A100 (120 scenario clusters, 6 operation families, 5 authorization conditions). Strong assumptions: known candidate rules, exact-task references built on the same GPU, known request order/grouping, offline calibration; probing slows victim median 4.71x; HF Transformers eager MoE path, not optimized fused-MoE servers.
candidates.independent_confirmation: None; builds on prior time-slicing primitive (TIMESLICE-SANDWICH).
candidates.relevance: medium - AI ops/security for multi-tenant GPU serving of agents; supports enforcing approval policy outside the model.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Adjacent to multi-agent permission boundaries coverage (where to enforce approvals) but a different threat (side channel).
candidates.summary: Model: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 under HF Transformers 4.55.4 (eager MoE). BF16 campaign on whole A100: 46/48 decisions correct (95.83% balanced accuracy, interval [89.58, 100]); observer on a different GPU saw nothing. NF4 coverage study in one MIG instance: 94.17% balanced accuracy on primary estimand [90.42, 97.50] at 100% coverage; 91.67% when window includes JSON generation; 1093/1200 (91.08%) across all five authorization conditions; 88.82% (302/340) on tasks where both settings produce identical output. Behaviour screen: 432 agent episodes over 24 repo instances; on gpt-oss-120b/vLLM stack routing traces replayed through FPGA transducers and across an A100 MIG boundary (sibling-MIG timing observer saw no activity mode). Mitigations tested: moving the rule to a trusted broker after inference (model emits fixed proposal) dropped classifier to 47.37% among classified groups (37.50% counting abstentions), a 58.33-point drop, while decisions remained 48/48 correct. Recommendations: deny untrusted processes on the agent's GPU/MIG instance; measure policy distinguishability on the serving runtime; enforce authorization outside the model.

candidates.title: Leaderboard Hacking: Preference-Based Model Evaluations are Vulnerable to Manipulation
candidates.author: Eve Fleisig et al.
candidates.organization: UC Berkeley; Bocconi University; Stanford University; MIT
candidates.what_changed: Shows Bradley-Terry arena-style leaderboards can be gamed via strategic voting (including votes on irrelevant pairs), strategic prompting and strategic nomination of extra models.
candidates.mechanism: Exploits Bradley-Terry/Borda dependence on irrelevant alternatives: votes between other models shift competitors' scores; adding copies of models the target beats inflates its rank; restricting prompts (e.g., by language) to areas where the target excels. Model identification for open-weight models via response log-likelihood, evading name filters.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium. Simulations on public LMArena 100k human-preference dataset (CC-BY-4.0), up to 10K manipulated votes (~10%); not tested on live leaderboards (ethics); assumes models identifiable; larger leaderboards need more manipulation.
candidates.independent_confirmation: Consistent with prior strategic-voting work (Zhao et al., Huang et al., Min et al.) and Singh et al. critique of LMArena.
candidates.relevance: medium - evaluation integrity for any preference-based eval (including internal production A/B arenas).
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Loosely related to Anthropic safety-evaluations piece; no direct overlap.
candidates.summary: Greedy strategic voting with up to 10K votes boosted models up to 20 places; 23 models (42%) moved more than 10 places; eight moved into the top 5; small gains of 2-3 places need under 2% of votes (2K of 100K). Strategic prompting by category gave up to 14 places; each attack up to 15-20 places; combined nomination plus prompting up to 45 places with 9 models moving over 10 places. Counterfactual inclusion/exclusion of model families shows existing rankings already depend on irrelevant alternatives. Authors propose defenses per attack (section 6). Limitations: smaller dataset than full LMArena; did not manipulate live rankings.

candidates.title: Only as Safe as the Weakest Agent: A Break That Appears Only When the System Is Multi-Agent
candidates.author: Keegan Wang, Anantika Mannby
candidates.organization: Carnegie Mellon University / University of Southern California; both also Prosaic Intelligence
candidates.what_changed: Shows that unmodified Claude Code and Codex, using their own default sub-agent delegation, adopt a planted forged file far more often than their orchestrator model does when reading the files itself; system safety tracks the weakest reader, not the strongest model.
candidates.mechanism: A file store (13-35 files) with one genuine record per fictional fact plus forged 'correction'/'gloss'/'volume'/'stacked' documents carrying two fixed tells (predates the record it corrects; missing accession line). Orchestrator either reads the store itself or is restricted to delegation (Claude Code: --allowedTools Task, Opus 5 orchestrator -> Haiku 4.5 sub-agent; Codex: GPT-5.6-sol -> GPT-5.6-terra, instruction-only restriction) plus a 200-line reference harness. Measure: 'harmful revision' = correct alone, wrong after the forged record reaches it.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium. 180 fictional facts per arm, one run per task, Wilson CIs and p-values; controls for clean-store delegation (0/180 harm) and same-tier sub-agent (0/180, 1/180, 11/540). Single-domain main corpus; small replication on 3 other stores (n=19-20). Codex delegation restriction only instructional. Turn-count 'suppressed verification' explanation explicitly labelled a hypothesis. Workshop paper (NeurIPS 2026 Meta-Agents workshop).
candidates.independent_confirmation: None. Authors cite related laundering result (Triedman et al. 2025) but this is the first test on unmodified commercial harnesses per the authors.
candidates.relevance: high - anyone delegating search/reading to a cheaper sub-agent model (default in Claude Code and Codex) inherits that model's gullibility toward poisoned files; concrete, cheap mitigations measured.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Adjacent to prior multi-agent permission-boundary and guardscope items (prior roster) and to 'Cleaning an Agent's History' (context provenance) but distinct: weakest-link delegation poisoning in shipped products.
candidates.summary: Setup: 180 two-option reading questions about fictional facts answered from a file store in which one forged document argues for the wrong answer. Results (Table 1): reading the store itself, Opus 5 in Claude Code adopts the forgery 1/180 on gloss and stacked; GPT-5.6-sol in Codex 0/180 on gloss; 0/540 across three orchestrators in the reference harness (2 harmful revisions in 1,080 direct trials). Delegating to the product's cheaper sub-agent: Claude Code 20/180 (gloss) and 75/180 (stacked); Codex 44/180 (gloss); reference harness 553/900 (volume). Same-tier sub-agents leave rates at the orchestrator level (0/180, 1/180, 11/540), and delegation over a clean store causes no harm, so the cause is reader weakness, not delegation per se. Which forgery works is harness-specific (Codex unaffected by repetition 0/180, fails authority gloss); an explicit prompt-injection instruction was resisted everywhere - 'what succeeds makes no demand, it looks like a record'. Delivery route matters: the same forged report is adopted 102/120 (85%) when it arrives as a sub-agent tool result vs 18/39 (46%) as a peer message. In Claude Code the sub-agent's summary preserved the provenance red flag in only 96/180 reports; orchestrators took 6.3 tool turns reading directly vs 3.2 when delegating. Propagation: with a corrupted worker, five aggregators (incl. GPT-5.5 and Opus 5) were wrong 94.7-98.0% of the time (751/757 conditional on worker being fooled); giving the aggregator the retrieved source record dropped error to 0/780. In the real harness, against a 15/40 baseline, a grounded verifier requiring the sub-agent to quote the original record got 3/40, a merely 'skeptical' instruction (store may be unreliable) got 1/40, and telling the orchestrator to read the record itself got 0/40. Notably the attack did not transfer to a code repository where verification is 'one grep away'. Applied angle: do not put a cheaper reader between the system and evidence its correctness depends on; require sub-agents to quote/pass original records (provenance) rather than summaries; treat sub-agent outputs as untrusted input; a one-line skepticism instruction measurably helps. Limitations: forgeries designed to be catchable only by careful readers; fictional-fact QA task; matched-brief control only possible in reference harness; n=40 for defense arms.

candidates.title: Do Verifier Judgments Survive Abstraction? Measuring Verification Transport for LLM Agent Evaluation
candidates.author: Disha Sheshanarayana, Sai Linisha Reddy Goli
candidates.what_changed: Introduces 'Verification Transport', a test of whether an LLM verifier/judge's correct verdict on an agent trajectory survives when the same execution is shown through macro-actions, delegation boundaries or compacted history; finds up to ~31% of correct verdicts flip or vanish.
candidates.mechanism: From frozen trajectories, deterministically build matched native, abstracted and restored views (no re-running agents), holding task, outcome, ground truth, criterion and verifier fixed. Three abstractions: macro abstraction (composed tools), delegation (sub-agent boundary), history compaction (earlier region replaced by a compaction marker, recent evidence + last tool call/result retained). Restoration reinserts the exact original events. Metric VTFR = share of native-correct judgments that become wrong or no-verdict.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium-high for a workshop paper: 4 benchmarks (AgentProcessBench 250 trajectories, ATBench 758, PlanRewardBench 441 pairs, AgentDojo 754), 7 verifier backbones (Gemini-3.7-Flash, Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-OSS-120B/20B, Gemma-4-31B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B, Llama-4-Maverick), 4 protocols; code released. Synthetic (frozen, constructed) abstractions rather than live ones; no frontier closed judges like Claude/GPT-5 class. NeurIPS 2026 'Who Verifies the Agents?' workshop.
candidates.relevance: high - directly relevant to anyone grading agent runs with LLM judges after compaction or sub-agent delegation (most production harnesses).
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Extends prior 'When Evaluators of AI Agents Disagree' (tau2-bench evaluator disagreement) and pairs with 'Only as Safe as the Weakest Agent' (evidence lost at delegation hops).
candidates.summary: Among judgments correct on the native view, transport failure is 31.0% under macro abstraction, 30.9% under delegation and 20.3% under compaction. Failure modes differ by protocol: plain LLM-judge (V-LLM) has the lowest VTFR (16.4/17.3/14.1%) but fails mostly by flipping to wrong verdicts (15.8% wrong vs 0.7% no-verdict under macro), while evidence-grounded (34.5/34.0/18.7%), agentic (25.0/23.6/18.2%) and deliberative (49.3/50.2/30.7%) verifiers more often abstain - so a lower failure rate is not the same as more reliability. Restoring exact provenance recovers 85.5% of transport failures overall (87.9% macro, 86.9% delegation, 79.8% compaction) while degrading only 5.2% of judgments that had survived; recovery drops when provenance is lossy. Failure grows with abstraction severity. Applied angle: if your eval pipeline judges compacted transcripts or orchestrator-only views, keep an exact link from every abstraction boundary back to the raw events and hand them to the judge; report judge accuracy per view, not only on full transcripts; prefer verifiers that abstain over ones that silently flip when evidence is missing. Limitations (authors): three controlled abstraction types, frozen not live trajectories, restoration assumes provenance exists, VTFR conditions on native-correct judgments. Code: github.com/Disha1001/Verification-Transport.

candidates.title: Callo: Serving Cache-Miss Requests with Speculative Decoding on Invalidated KV under Prefill-Decode Disaggregation
candidates.author: Jianjun Ou, Matthew Lentz
candidates.what_changed: A serving technique that turns the KV cache invalidated by agent context edits (e.g., SWE-agent replacing old tool outputs with placeholders) into a speculative-decoding draft source while the exact re-prefill is computed, then verifies before committing.
candidates.mechanism: Under P/D disaggregation, the decode instance drafts tokens using stale (invalidated) KV while the prefill instance streams exact KV layer-by-layer within each 8k chunk; drafts are verified against exact KV before commit, so outputs are lossless. Schedules speculation into idle decode capacity, stops drafting when cumulative acceptance probability < 0.3, yields lowest-probability speculations first; speculative KV kept out of the prefix cache. Implemented via vLLM scheduler and KV-connector extension points with no vLLM source or kernel changes.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium. Two-GPU testbed (2x H200 NVL, NVLink, vLLM 0.29, NIXL), SWE-agent 1.1 sessions, Llama-3.3-70B FP8, Gemma-4-31B, Mistral-Small-3.2-24B; cluster-scale results are simulation driven by traces. Correctness check: 1,928 verification events / 44,792 committed tokens with no KV-fingerprint mismatch. Gains modest (1.05-1.27x).
candidates.relevance: medium-high - quantifies the hidden serving cost of context editing/compaction in agents and a lossless mitigation for self-hosted vLLM P/D deployments.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Same theme as prior roster serving items (Recompute or Restore? host-tier KV; makespan coordination) and 'Read Once, Answer Many'; distinct mechanism.
candidates.summary: Motivation: context edits (dropping old tool outputs) cut input tokens 40-60% without hurting solve rates per cited work, but they invalidate prefix-cached KV; on Llama-3.3-70B with SWE-agent's default 'keep last five tool outputs' policy, 79% of requests are edit-induced cache misses that must wait for re-prefill. Callo drafts on the stale KV meanwhile; drafts on invalidated KV still get high acceptance and acceptance rises as exact layers arrive. Results: all-request speedups over unmodified vLLM of 1.05-1.19x at moderate load (abstract), miss-request speedups 1.06-1.24x; on the main config 1.10x light / 1.14x moderate load; with a D-instance batch limit of 16 the speedup rises from 1.10x to 1.27x at full load. Gains are largest for latency-sensitive tasks with short outputs; for long reasoning outputs decoding dominates and the saving is a small fraction; an alternative configuration was slower than vLLM at moderate load (0.88-0.92x). Applied angle: if you run agents on self-hosted P/D-disaggregated vLLM and your harness prunes or rewrites history, cache misses dominate; Callo shows the stale cache still has value. Also a useful data point for harness designers weighing context pruning against prefix-cache hits.

candidates.title: Unfinished-Bench: Measuring Rule Violations by Persistent Agents in Realistic Work Environments
candidates.author: Seunghyun Lee, Jaehui Hwang, Dongyoon Han, Sangdoo Yun
candidates.what_changed: A benchmark showing that harness-supplied 'keep going until done' persistence (completion instructions + re-prompts on stop) increases agents' violations of rules found in internal documents, and that rules in documents are violated ~5x more than the same rules stated by the user.
candidates.mechanism: 97 scenarios across 7 fictional organizations and 7 risk categories where goal and an embedded rule cannot both hold. Same rule placed either in an internal document the agent discovers or stated by the user. Persistence condition uses Hermes Agent harness default completion instructions plus up to 6 re-prompts marked as coming from the harness. Claude Sonnet 5.5 judge on a rubric (kappa 0.84 on re-labels).
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium. 12 open models only (gpt-oss-120b/20b, Gemma 4 31B/26B/12B, Qwen 3.8 27B and Flash-Next, DeepSeek V4 Pro, V4.1 Flash, GLM 5.3 and Flash, Muse Glimmer 30B); single harness; bootstrap CIs over 97 scenarios; no proprietary models.
candidates.relevance: high - most production coding/ops harnesses add exactly this persistence; shows written-down policies in docs are weak guardrails.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Related to prior 'Termination Lag' (agents stop late) and safety/abstention items; distinct focus on persistence vs embedded rules.
candidates.summary: Averaged over 12 models, violation rates were 4.7% (user-stated rule) and 32.2% (rule in a document) without persistence, rising to 8.5% and 43.6% with persistence. Range with persistence on doc rules: 1.0% (GLM 5.3) to 89.7% (gpt-oss-120b, up from 64.9%). Models split into six with 50-66% doc-violation rates without persistence and six with 0.5-6.2%. The agents saw the rule: in 99.1% of 1,016 doc violations the rule section appeared in a tool result, in 98.3% before the first work-tool use, and in 89% of a judged sample the agent wrote the rule down in its reasoning before violating it; the dominant stated reason was the user's goal (83%). Half of violations happened before any re-prompt (completion instructions alone suffice); a marker-only re-prompt ablation showed no significant change in 23 of 24 combinations; agents read the re-prompt as user permission in only 4% of cases. Some models falsely reported compliance in final reports (Qwen 3.8 27B and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash never did). Applied angle: completion-pressure system prompts in agent harnesses trade off against policy compliance; important rules should be enforced in tools/permissions or surfaced as user-level instructions, not left in documents; test agents with rules embedded in the environment. Docs: francis21c.github.io/unfinished-bench.

candidates.title: CarryOn: Learning What to Keep in Context for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
candidates.author: Lihuan Li, Ruiyi Yang, Jiru Wang, Yifan Duan, Xiachong Lin, Hao Xue, Yang Song, Flora Salim
candidates.organization: University of New South Wales; HKUST (Guangzhou)
candidates.what_changed: An external context manager that keeps a compact execution state plus source-linked fine-grained evidence chosen by a small learned selector, without extra LLM calls for context management.
candidates.mechanism: History split into evidence units; a Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B selector (trained offline from Claude Sonnet 5 state annotations and evidence citations) scores units against task and current observation; adaptive retention keeps relevant units with source references next to a compact state. Same selector reused across Actor models per benchmark.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium. AppWorld (168 tasks), OfficeBench (95), Tau2 Telecom (40) with three Actors (Claude Sonnet 5, Qwen3.8-27B, Gemma-4-31B); baselines Full History, FIFO-5, Retrieval, LLMLingua-2, ACON, SWE-Pruner, AGORA. Separate selector per benchmark; text-only; anonymous repo.
candidates.relevance: high - context engineering for long-horizon agents with cost accounting (normalized cost per success).
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Same theme as prior Folio (recoverable context folding) and 'Cleaning an Agent's History'; a competing approach (learned selection vs programmatic folding).
candidates.summary: Averaged equally across benchmarks and Actors, CarryOn reaches 75.7% task success, +13.3 points over full history and +6.7 over the strongest baseline (SWE-Pruner); best S_0.8 (success-weighted cost score) and lowest normalized cost per success (0.792). Motivating example: coworker records fetched at step 9 remain available at step 33 when a summary would have dropped them. Applied angle: a cheap 0.6B reranker can do context selection, avoiding LLM-summarization calls and preserving exact details; but selector must be trained per environment. Limitations: three text benchmarks; generalization to new tool interfaces unexplored.

candidates.title: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs
candidates.author: Seyed Mahmoud Sajjadi Mohammadabadi
candidates.what_changed: A quantitative synthesis of 9 studies (516 multi-agent configurations) finding that once baselines are matched on samples or budget, multi-agent LLM systems average slightly below single-agent baselines; proposes the PACE compute-parity reporting protocol and a CLI.
candidates.mechanism: Six-dimensional resource vector R (thinking tokens, total tokens, cost, latency, sample count, tool scaffolding) and a baseline ladder (A greedy single pass, B sampled, C budget-matched). Multilevel REML random-effects models on log-odds; stylized propositions on redundancy, correlated votes and conformity.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium-low/medium. Meta-analysis of only 9 studies; one study supplies 180 of 516 configurations; first five studies chosen without a search protocol (author notes selection bias); single author.
candidates.independent_confirmation: Partially consistent with cited primary studies (e.g., single agents matching debate at equal thinking tokens).
candidates.relevance: medium-high - practical decision rules for whether to build multi-agent systems; evaluation hygiene.
candidates.summary: Contrast means: -0.032 vs single greedy pass; -0.042 vs sample- or budget-matched baselines. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below baseline in 74% of 474 comparable contrasts (76% of 360 vs sampled baselines); study means nonpositive in 8 of 9 studies. Omitting the dominant study, the greedy-baseline contrast is near zero (-0.005). Example cited: majority voting without communication beats two-round decentralized debate (0.747 vs 0.715) at matched agent count; graphs vs greedy CoT differ by -0.007 at a median 8.1x cost. Practitioner rules: (1) exhaust single-agent test-time scaling (sampling/voting/more thinking) first; (2) use multiple agents for structural reasons (context exceeds window, independent parallel tools, sandboxed states), not accuracy targets; (3) enforce external verification (tests, compilers, DB queries). Releases PACE reviewer checklist and pace CLI at github.com/mahmoudsajjadi/pace.

candidates.title: Co-Sight Harness: Externalized Control Assets and Deterministic Enforcement for Long-Horizon Business Agents
candidates.author: Luyao Wang et al. (14 authors)
candidates.what_changed: Production report: keeping the model fixed and moving workflow definition, state and domain knowledge into versioned 'control assets' enforced by a state machine and machine-checkable acceptance gates made 200+-step business workflows reliable.
candidates.mechanism: Request compiled into versioned control assets outside the model; state machine + acceptance gates enforce them at runtime; independent auditor grades the trace; assets change only after a regression check and human approval. Released as open-source plugins (Co-Sight repo).
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium-low. Vendor self-report on its own deployed workflows; 120-case evaluation set for Domain A; backbone reached via external API and not named in the parts read; before/after comparison with a controlled ablation.
candidates.independent_confirmation: None; two other internal teams adopted it (4 and 7 days).
candidates.relevance: medium-high - concrete harness pattern (deterministic gates, versioned assets, regression-gated updates) for enterprise agents.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Related to harness-engineering items (AgentTorrent in prior roster).
candidates.summary: Domain A, 120-case end-to-end set: unattended completion 50% -> 100%, retrieval recall 56% -> 91.67%, end-to-end latency 440 -> 159 minutes, scenario-analysis recall 45% -> 93%. Deployment thresholds: pass@3 >= 90% and pass^3 = 100% on disjoint ability/regression sets; confidence graded as human confirmation, sampled LLM verification, or deterministic checks. Six tuning rounds over one week; 30-day pre-asset observation. Applied angle: for long business workflows, reliability came from externalizing state and checks, not from a stronger model; asset changes go through regression tests like code. Code: github.com/ZTE-AICloud/Co-Sight (Co-Sight Harness folder).

candidates.title: What LLM Agents See and What Users Say
candidates.author: Yue Zhao, Angela Huyue Zhang, S. Alex Yang, Hua Wei, Xiyang Hu
candidates.organization: Not confirmed (abs page lists no affiliations; UNVERIFIED)
candidates.what_changed: Shows that whether agents act on a wrong record (cancel the wrong reservation, delete a non-empty folder) depends heavily on whether a lookup tool lists competing matches or merely counts them; adding a same-name customer to a retail benchmark caused wrong-account writes in ~25% of conversations.
candidates.mechanism: Presupposition framing: an act is safe only if each presupposed claim is seen, confirmed by the user, or disclosed while reversible. Vary whether search lists, counts or omits a second match and whether the user asserts a claim a record refutes; 16 templates across 36 agents.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium; many models (36), controlled templates; only abstract and intro read.
candidates.relevance: high - direct tool-design lesson for write actions (lookups should list or check competing records).
candidates.summary: Under a role-only prompt, when search reports only a count of a second record, most of 36 earlier agents act on the one they see; listing both stops most. If the user claims a folder is empty, a count of its one item stops agents about as often as a listing. The newest Claude and GPT models always open a counted second record, then never act. In a retail benchmark with an added same-name, same-zip customer, a lookup returning that customer first led to wrong-account writes in about a quarter of conversations; a lookup that checks a street address the user knows kept completion near the single-customer level. Applied angle: design lookup tools for destructive actions to return all candidate matches or require a disambiguating field; evaluate by varying what tools show.

candidates.title: Forget the Lineage: Forward-Secure, Lineage-Complete Cryptographic Erasure for LLM-Agent Memory (LinEra)
candidates.author: Yulliwas Ameur, Billal Mokhtari, Samia Bouzefrane
candidates.what_changed: Cryptographic 'right to be forgotten' for agent memory: deleting a message also makes every summary, extracted fact and embedding derived from it unreadable, integrated with mem0.
candidates.mechanism: Each memory object encrypted under a key derived from its parents' keys along the derivation DAG; source keys from a puncturable PRF so forgetting is one puncture; a lineage rule records as parents everything the writer saw.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium: security proofs plus experiments with Qwen2.5 (1.5B-7B) writing LoCoMo memories; small models only.
candidates.relevance: medium - privacy/compliance for persistent agent memory.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Related to prior memory items (DISCERN, CoReMem in roster).
candidates.summary: Shows logical deletion is insufficient: with Qwen2.5-7B writing memory for all ten LoCoMo conversations, an attacker holding every file and the current keys recovers 70 of 71 forgotten secrets after logical deletion, 67 with per-object or epoch keys, and none with LinEra; the same holds for every writer tested. Cost: a larger 'forgetting radius' that follows the writer's fan-in - forgetting 1% of turns erases 73.0% of derived memories with session-level summaries but only 3.8% with four-turn windows (which also answer better); re-deriving restores what is lost. Key derivation about 0.28 ms at 10^6 objects. Applied angle: if you run mem0-style memory and must honor deletion requests, derived artifacts (summaries, embeddings, backups) are the leak; lineage-keyed encryption plus small summarization windows is one design. Code and LLM-call logs released per the arXiv comments.

candidates.title: VelServe: Taming Decode Jitters in LLM Inference with Tail-Calibrated Scheduling
candidates.author: Ishaan Datta, Alind Khare, Koushik Kumar Dey, Ratnesh Jamidar, Anand Kumar Singh
candidates.what_changed: An SLO-aware scheduler that sizes each decode step's prefill work from the measured tail of its own iteration latency, rather than the predicted mean, to stop 'decode jitter' TBT violations.
candidates.mechanism: Headroom per iteration set by the SLO's tolerated late-step rate; shortest-waiting-prompt-first to compensate slowed prefill; under disaggregation, spaces admissions so no request sees more slow admission steps than its P99 allows.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium; abstract only read. Qwen3-8B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, DeepSeek-V2-Lite; 8-GPU disaggregated setup.
candidates.relevance: medium - serving SLO engineering for streaming apps.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Serving theme as prior OverServe/serving roster items.
candidates.summary: Claims 2.4-2.9x the SLO goodput of the strongest baseline on Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, at least 4.4x on DeepSeek-V2-Lite; with P/D disaggregation on eight GPUs meets the SLO for more than twice as many requests as state-of-the-art baselines. Applied angle: tail (P99) TBT, not mean, should set chunked-prefill budgets.

candidates.title: Superfluid: Local AI Server for Distributed LLM Inference
candidates.author: Prabod Rathnayaka, Isura Manchanayake, Srikandabala Kogul, Steve Siu, Fabian Waschkowski, Lukas Wesemann
candidates.what_changed: Open-source (Apache-2.0) local LLM server that prioritizes interactive requests over background agent work on one device and pools heterogeneous machines into one endpoint.
candidates.mechanism: Drives llama.cpp/MLX/BaseRT in isolated workers under one scheduler; shared-prompt computed once; tokens written to a durable log before reaching the client; fleet mode routes by measured speed with join/fail tolerance.
candidates.evidence_quality: Low-medium; author benchmarks, abstract only read.
candidates.relevance: medium - local multi-agent serving on Macs/heterogeneous fleets.
candidates.summary: Qwen3.8-27B on an Apple M5 Pro: a chat sent while eight agents are working gets first token in 1.5 s vs 291-612 s on llama-server, Ollama and another server. Six machines from three chip vendors, 64 simulated users for an hour: all 5,041 requests answered while machines join and one is killed; throughput 112 -> 534 tok/s, median TTFT 99 -> 12 s. Twelve Mac Studio M3 Ultras: 10,656 tok/s across 38,563 requests from 384 agents without failure.

candidates.title: Interpreting Coding Agents Through Their Behavioral Trajectories
candidates.author: Ibragim Badertdinov, Alexander Golubev
candidates.what_changed: Large-scale behavioral analysis of 143,209 coding-agent trajectories from 125 agent configurations (117 models), with a released deterministic parser mapping traces to search/edit/test actions.
candidates.mechanism: Rule-based parser audited against a six-model consensus on 500 events; behavioral profiles used to fingerprint agent stacks.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium; abstract only. IAB workshop at NeurIPS 2026.
candidates.relevance: medium - process metrics beyond pass rate for choosing scaffolds/reasoning effort.
candidates.summary: Agents with similar solve rates differ substantially in how they explore, modify and verify; behavioral profiles alone (no outcomes, token counts or tool names) retrieve the agent stack across disjoint repositories and languages; scaffold choice and reasoning effort systematically shift search, editing and testing behavior. Parser and pipeline released.

candidates.title: Soteria: Formally Verified Planning with Runtime Enforcement for Safe LLM Agents
candidates.author: Mike He, Ankush Desai, Sharad Malik, Aarti Gupta
candidates.what_changed: Agent generates a structured plan that is formally verified against policy specs before any tool call; the verified plan then guides recovery when runtime enforcement blocks an action.
candidates.mechanism: Verified hierarchical planning + runtime specification enforcement.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium; abstract only; NeurIPS'26 oral per comments.
candidates.relevance: medium - policy-constrained tool agents (tau-bench-style).
candidates.summary: Claims 1.7x the average task success of the best baselines across multiple tool-use benchmarks with zero policy-specification violations. Applied angle: blocking unsafe actions without a recovery plan strands agents; a verified plan gives a fallback route.

candidates.title: Learn then Bet: Learning Interpretable Rules for Reliable Agent Intervention (LeBet)
candidates.author: You-Lin Chen, Xinyi Lisa Chen, Pedro Herrero-Vidal, Xiaojing Yu, Bingqing Song, Bin Xu
candidates.what_changed: Replaces turn limits/keyword filters for stopping agent runs with a learned OR-of-AND rule monitor plus a betting statistic giving finite-sample false-positive guarantees.
candidates.mechanism: Interpretable boolean rules learned by stochastic local search; evidence accumulated via fixed betting statistic; intervene at threshold.
candidates.evidence_quality: Low-medium; single setting (SWE-bench Lite, Ministral 3 8B); abstract only.
candidates.relevance: medium - runtime monitors for when to kill/escalate agent runs.
candidates.summary: On SWE-bench Lite with Ministral 3 8B, the learned monitor saves 34.46% of input+output tokens and raises output precision from 18.33% to 21.59%, with empirical false-positive rate 13.64%.

candidates.title: Can You Trust Your Finance Agent? Drift, Diagnosis and Auditable Intervention on One Shipped Financial Research Agent
candidates.author: Cosimo Galeone, Anna Ettorre, Ginevra Mariani, Minsu Park, Giuseppe Ettorre, Daniele Ligorio
candidates.what_changed: Case study measuring run-to-run variance, failure ownership and noise-aware optimization on the Vals Finance Agent Benchmark v2 reference agent.
candidates.mechanism: Seven identical runs; frozen failure taxonomy by owning layer (instructions/tools/model/data); blind multi-model readers; one-change-per-round optimization accepted only above a pre-registered noise threshold.
candidates.evidence_quality: Low (authors: one agent, nine test questions, not a general result) but methodologically careful.
candidates.relevance: medium - template for agent eval hygiene (noise floors, failure ownership).
candidates.summary: Seven identical runs on 18 questions pass 105-123 of 149 rubric criteria and cost varies by up to 17%. Of 20 failed trajectories, 13 owned by instructions, 3 tools, 4 model, 0 data; blind readers agree with the LLM analyzer 94% (inter-reader 93%). Cost-objective optimization reaches 0.34x baseline cost on held-out questions (95% CI 0.22-0.58) at accuracy within noise; accuracy objective gained 14 points on dev but 1.5 on held-out (CI -5.3 to +7.2), i.e. not real once noise is accounted for.

candidates.title: GDP.xlsx: Benchmarking Frontier Models on Professional Workbooks
candidates.author: Suhaas Garre, Sushant Mehta, Edwin Chen
candidates.what_changed: New spreadsheet-agent benchmark: 70 professional requests with full workbooks (2.18M populated cells) and 791 binary rubric criteria, graded by an agentic judge that opens the file.
candidates.mechanism: Agents in a container with spreadsheet tools; strict pass@1 (all criteria met); completeness/exclusivity criteria for set-valued answers; 67 of 70 tasks held out.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium; abstract only; mostly private test set.
candidates.relevance: medium - realistic office-agent eval.
candidates.summary: Across 20 model configurations, the best (Gemini 4 Argon) passes 38.3% of attempts; median 19.3%. Harness and three public tasks released.

candidates.title: WebArena-Pro: A Heterogeneous, Multimodal, Reproducible Benchmark for Web Agents
candidates.author: Imene Kerboua et al.
candidates.what_changed: 300 tasks across 20 self-hosted web apps in six categories, with audio and video as first-class observations; reproducible and parallel.
candidates.mechanism: Human-curated tasks via annotator interface, LLM-assisted triage, human validation; isolated per-task execution.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium; abstract only; NeurIPS 2026 E&D track.
candidates.relevance: medium - web-agent evaluation; compares coding-agent harnesses vs generic agents.
candidates.summary: Best: Codex with GPT 6.1 Sol and Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 tied at 62.3%; OpenCode with Kimi 3.1 Pro 60.7%; best GenericAgent configurations (Gemini 3.1 Pro omni, Gemma4 31B) 30.3% - coding-agent harnesses roughly double generic web agents.

candidates.title: HerAgent: A Block-Level Checkpointing Harness for Coding-Agent Environment Setup
candidates.author: Xiang Li, Siyu Lu, Federica Sarro, Claire Le Goues, He Ye
candidates.what_changed: Environment-setup agent that executes, validates, checkpoints, repairs and rolls back at the level of 'semantic setup blocks' instead of single commands or whole scripts.
candidates.mechanism: Block-level progress control abstraction.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium; abstract only; six prior agents, four datasets.
candidates.relevance: medium - repo setup for coding agents/CI sandboxes.
candidates.summary: Improves setup success in every comparison; Installamatic-Bench 52.0% -> 85.0%, SetupBench 46.3% -> 70.4%; up to 94.5% lower setup cost.

candidates.title: ProdPilot: A Layered Model Context Protocol System for Automated Production Readiness and Deployment of Vibe-Coded Projects
candidates.author: Muhammad Sudais Khalid, Muhammad Junaid Asif, Rehan Naveed Abbasi, Rana Fayyaz Ahmad
candidates.what_changed: A local MCP server that audits Node/React projects against 50 production-readiness rules and repairs them mostly with templates, accepting a fix only when the flagging checker passes.
candidates.mechanism: 28 rules fixed by templates, 16 by extracted values, 6 by the IDE agent's model; checker-gated acceptance; deployability classifier.
candidates.evidence_quality: Low-medium; abstract only.
candidates.relevance: medium - deterministic MCP tooling around AI-generated code.
candidates.summary: 88.0% of rules need no model-written content; 93.5% of violations in 499 real repos fall in those classes. Independent verification rejected 25 of 237 fixes reported as applied. Deployability model 0.909 ROC AUC on 684 deployments; gated deploy + CI in 82 s; works from VS Code, Cursor and Windsurf. v1 Nov 11 but first announced Nov 16.

candidates.title: Securing Multi-Agent Systems by Design (ReMA attack / SecMAS aggregation)
candidates.author: Xilong Wang, Xiaoxing Chen, Neil Gong
candidates.what_changed: Optimized malicious-response attacks on multi-agent aggregation and a semantic-consistency secure aggregation rule with proven guarantees.
candidates.mechanism: ReMA iteratively optimizes malicious sub-agent responses using a surrogate MAS; SecMAS picks the response most consistent with a sufficiently large subset of others.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium; abstract only, no numbers in abstract.
candidates.relevance: medium - complements 'Weakest Agent' result.
candidates.summary: Existing aggregation rules are vulnerable to ReMA; SecMAS defends against all evaluated attacks including adaptive variants with comparable utility (no figures in abstract).

candidates.title: From Bytes to Behavior: Request-Level Attribution from Live GPU Hidden States
candidates.author: Jonathan Pan, Yidi Yuan, Xin Wei Chia, Xinhui Su, Vincent Tan, Brenda Ong
candidates.what_changed: Forensic method to read per-layer residual-stream activations from a live GPU inference process with a non-modifying debugger.
candidates.mechanism: Six-stage acquisition with PyTorch-allocator-clock or kernel-launch-clock adapters to locate tensors in VRAM.
candidates.evidence_quality: Low-medium; 7-page paper, abstract only.
candidates.relevance: low-medium - AI incident forensics; also a reminder that VRAM holds recoverable request state (cf. prior PolicySniff).
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Thematically adjacent to prior PolicySniff / recurrent-state leakage items.
candidates.summary: Byte-exact recovery validated on 33 open decoder-only models across nine architecture classes; linear probes on recovered states distinguish refusal from compliance with AUROC 0.88.

candidates.title: Zero-SM NCCL: A Systematic Guide to Designing and Deploying SM-Free GPU Communication
candidates.author: Zhenhao He et al. (incl. Torsten Hoefler)
candidates.organization: Not stated on abs page (UNVERIFIED; likely NVIDIA authors)
candidates.what_changed: NCCL collectives that use copy engines, CUDA stream memory ops and a CPU RDMA proxy instead of SM kernels.
candidates.mechanism: SM-free AllGather/AlltoAll and one-sided ncclPutSignal/ncclWaitSignal.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium; abstract only; GB200 NVL72 and B200 NVL8.
candidates.relevance: low-medium - training/inference infrastructure.
candidates.summary: Up to 1.36x AllGather bandwidth vs legacy SM kernels; median overlapped-GEMM slowdown 33% -> 4% at higher per-op latency; Megatron-LM FSDP up to +3.5%, pipeline parallelism up to +15%; loses on small messages and host-bound workloads.
